proxy_port.description: Reverse proxy port for the Home Assistant link. Advanced; set it only when your own proxy fronts this panel on another port.
proxy_port.title: Proxy port

expose.description: Which addresses the panel answers on. 'all' serves it on every interface, including in the clear on the LAN. 'proxy' limits it to the loopback and the Docker bridge, so it is reachable over TLS on the proxy port or through an SSH tunnel, and not otherwise. The proxy reaches the panel over the loopback when Caddy runs as a system service, or over the Docker bridge when it runs in a container; Node-RED always uses the bridge.
expose.title: Expose

enabled.markdownDescription:
Enable cloud registration

When enabled, device registers with boneIO Cloud API and downloads
wildcard SSL certificate for *.black.boneio.app domain.
This allows PWA installation on mobile devices.
enabled.title: Enabled

declined.markdownDescription:
Not interested in cloud registration

Set this when you have decided against registering with boneIO
Cloud. Registration publishes this device's local address in DNS,
which is a reasonable thing to refuse — and without somewhere to
record the refusal the panel goes on recommending it, so the
certificate check can never be settled.

It changes nothing about how the device works. It only stops the
panel offering cloud registration as the way to a trusted
certificate, leaving uploading your own.
declined.title: Declined

map_tiles.description: Allow the location picker to load a map
map_tiles.markdownDescription:
Allow the location picker to load a map

Off by default. When on, the Location page can show an
OpenStreetMap map to pick the coordinates from, and the panel's
Content-Security-Policy gains the OpenStreetMap tile servers in
its `img-src` directive.

That is a real loosening, not a formality. An image URL is an
outbound channel: someone who already had script execution in the
panel could encode data into a tile path and read it out of
someone else's access log. The map is a convenience, so it is
opt-in and nobody pays for it who is not using it.

The tiles are fetched by your browser, not by the controller, so
this works on a device with no route to the internet — as long as
the computer you open the panel from has one. Without a map the
coordinates can still be typed in, or filled from the timezone.

Tiles come from openstreetmap.org, which sees the area you are
looking at. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors.
map_tiles.title: Map tiles

frame_ancestors.description: Which sites may embed this panel in a frame
frame_ancestors.markdownDescription:
Which sites may embed this panel in a frame

Sets the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive, which
is what protects the panel from clickjacking.

Unset means `self` since 1.6: only this device may frame the
panel. That is also what the boneIO Black add-on for Home
Assistant needs — its nginx proxies each controller, so the
framed page is served on Home Assistant's own origin and is
same-origin with the dashboard framing it.

A list of plain tokens. Write `self`, not `'self'` — the quotes
CSP wants are added when the header is built, so nothing here
has to survive YAML stripping them:

  frame_ancestors:
    - self

Add an address when a dashboard frames this device directly, with
an iframe card or panel_iframe rather than through the add-on:

  frame_ancestors:
    - self
    - https://homeassistant.local:8123

A single `*` lifts the restriction entirely. It cannot be
combined — alongside it, every other entry means nothing.

A plain string still works, so configs written before the list
existed keep loading. The Security section in the panel edits
this without the syntax.

X-Frame-Options is deliberately not sent: it cannot name an
allowed origin, so it could not express the ingress case.
frame_ancestors.title: Frame ancestors

allow_anonymous.description: Allow unauthenticated access to the web UI and API
allow_anonymous.markdownDescription:
Allow unauthenticated access to the web UI and API

DANGEROUS. Leave this off unless you know why you need it.

From 1.6 a device with no administrator account refuses API
requests until the first-run wizard has been completed. Setting
this to true restores the pre-1.6 behaviour: anyone who can reach
the device on the network can read its configuration, switch its
outputs and reboot it, with no password.

It exists for headless provisioning and for installations where
authentication is already enforced in front of boneIO (for
example a reverse proxy or Home Assistant ingress). The device
logs a warning on every start while this is on.
allow_anonymous.title: Allow anonymous
